newsitem.title: USA: Coffee and precious metals rise, oil prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Coffee and precious metals rise, oil prices fall.

text.p: Coffee prices rose Friday as traders continued to worry about lower supplies this year from Latin America and most precious metals also rose on concerns about a possible rise in interest rates.
In other markets, soybean prices rose and oil prices fell. Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 commodity futures fell 0.31 point to 242.41 points.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, traders shrugged off talk that Brazilian coffee supplies will not be as tight as expected. May futures closed 5.75 cents a pound higher at 176.85 cents, just below the life-of-contract high.
Traders said talk that influential consultant Leon Yallouz had forecast next season's Brazilian harvest at around 27.5 million 132-pound bags weighed on coffee prices early.
Brazilian traders have been expecting that crop to total from 20 million to 23 million bags. Yallouz would not comment on the contents of his report but confirmed it was issued Thursday.
But professional speculators saw the pullback in prices as a buying opportunity in both coffee options and futures based on current tight physical stocks of coffee.
That supportive factor was underlined after the close of trading as the CSCE reported coffee stocks certified for delivery in warehouses fell by 11,250 bags overnight, or 43 percent, to 14,545 bags.
Colombia, the second largest coffee producer after Brazil, also announced it raised its domestic coffee price by 5.48 percent to an all-time high of 327,250 pesos per 275-pounds.
"The market keeps going up on its own momentum," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "As long as it points higher it is going to continue to draw in speculators."
Precious metals ended mostly higher, with COMEX April gold up $4.10 an ounce at $365.10, an eight-week high. May silver closed 6.5 cents an ounce higher at $5.360.

Weakness in U.S. stock and bond prices this week provided some support for hard assets like gold and silver after Federal Reserve chairman Greenspan warned about excessive valuations and suggested interest rates may need to be raised preemptively to combat potential inflation.

Both metals were also buoyed by strength in the platinum group this week due to the threat of a strike at Russia's big Norilsk mine on March 15 and a cutoff of Russian shipments to Japanese manufacturers this month.
NYMEX April platinum ended up 10 cents at $396.40 but well off the day's highs at $415.00 an ounce. In the physical market, however, platinum was quoted at $398.75 in London, a seven-month high.

Russia is the world's main supplier of palladium and the second largest supplier of platinum, while Japan is the world's largest consumer of both metals. But annual talks on the Russia/Japan supply contract broke down in Decemmber.
"There have been no shipments of palladium to Japan since January causing many fabricators to turn to the spot market for the metal they need," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.

News on Friday of significant imports of platinum and palladium into Japan in January, including supplies from Russia, suggested Japanese stocks may not have been drawn down as much as earlier expected, however.
June palladium closed down $2.40 an ounce at $155.05.
NYMEX crude oil prices fell to their lowest level since July as speculators continued to bail out of the market with adequate supplies and mild winter weather sparking the sales.
April crude ended 59 cents lower at $20.30 a barrel, the lowest settlement for spot delivery futures since July 29.

"We went down a lot at the end with a Wall Street player a heavy seller of April which pushed it through $20.50. After that, stops were triggered and everyone just nailed it," said a New York crude dealer.
March gasoline ended down 1.02 cents a gallon at 61.65 cents and March heating oil down 1.27 cents at 54.76 cents.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans closed 9-1/4 cents per bushel higher at $7.93-1/4 as a late flurry of buying by professional speculators fed the gains. Recent fund buying of grains ahead of spring planting continued strong.
March corn ended 3/4 cent a bushel higher at $2.96-3/4.
